questions.passage: The philosopher Ruth Millikan proposed that the meaning of a mental representation derives not from its internal structure but from the evolutionary function it was selected to perform. A frog's neural “bug detector,” on this view, means small dark moving thing not because of what it resembles but because detecting such things is what natural selection shaped it to do. Meaning, in other words, is fixed by history rather than by present resemblance—an account that dissolves puzzles about how a misfiring detector can still mean anything at all.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It raises an objection that the final sentence goes on to rebut.
It introduces a competing theory of meaning that the text ultimately favors.
It provides a concrete illustration of the general principle stated in the preceding sentence.
It qualifies the preceding sentence by noting an exception to the principle it states.

questions.passage: Archaeologists have long debated why the Norse settlements in Greenland collapsed around 1450. One historian argues that the settlers' insistence on a European-style cattle-and-hay economy, rather than adaptation to marine hunting, doomed them. Had the Norse relied more heavily on seals and fish, this argument holds, their colonies might well have endured the cooling climate.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the underlined claim?
options: The neighboring Thule Inuit, whose economy centered on marine hunting, persisted in the same region throughout the very cooling that coincided with the Norse collapse.
Isotopic analysis of Norse skeletons shows that the share of marine food in the diet rose steadily in the decades before the collapse, yet the settlements still failed.
Written records show that the Norse regarded seal meat as a food of last resort, eaten only in years of famine.
Pollen cores indicate that the hay meadows near the settlements remained productive until the final years of occupation.

questions.passage: Policymakers frequently assume that giving people more information will lead them to make better choices. Yet in several controlled studies, consumers presented with exhaustive product disclosures made worse decisions than those given a brief summary did, apparently because the flood of detail obscured the few factors that actually mattered. The finding suggests that the design of information—what is emphasized, and what is left out—can matter as much as its accuracy.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers an example that confirms the assumption described in the first sentence.
It presents evidence that unsettles a common assumption, motivating the conclusion drawn in the final sentence.
It defines a term that the remainder of the text goes on to apply.
It concedes a limitation of the studies that the text otherwise relies on.

questions.passage: Elinor received the news with a smile so composed that Mrs. Hartright was reassured, and went away satisfied that the girl had no great feeling in the matter. Yet when the door had closed, Elinor did not move for a long while; and when at last she crossed to the window, it was not the departing carriage she watched, but the long avenue of limes down which, in other years, she had walked believing the place, and everything in it, to be in some sense her own.
questions.question: Which choice best describes what the text most strongly suggests about Elinor?
options: She is relieved to be leaving a place that holds unhappy memories for her.
She resents Mrs. Hartright for failing to recognize her years of service.
She doubts that she will be able to find another position quickly.
Her outward calm conceals a deeper attachment to the house than she has let anyone see.

questions.passage: It is often said that the honeybee waggle dance tells foragers where to find flowers. But the dance's information is remarkably imprecise—recruits following it locate the advertised site only a fraction of the time—and colonies deprived of the dance's directional content forage nearly as efficiently in many landscapes. What the dance reliably conveys is not a map but a motivation: it excites nestmates and biases them toward searching, so that its principal value may lie less in the coordinates it encodes than in the collective attention it mobilizes.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The honeybee waggle dance may function less as a set of precise directions than as a means of rousing foragers to search.
The honeybee waggle dance communicates the location of flowers with a high degree of accuracy.
Honeybee colonies that cannot perform the waggle dance are unable to forage effectively.
Researchers have not yet determined what information, if any, the waggle dance conveys.

questions.passage: Frey spoke of the vineyard as one speaks of a patient not expected to recover: with tenderness, and without hope. Anselm said little. But each morning he was among the vines before the mist had lifted, and the neighbors, who had prophesied ruin for the brothers within the year, began to remark that the rows nearest the road, at least, had never in their memory been so faithfully tended.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: In contrast to Frey's spoken resignation, Anselm's diligent labor suggests a hope he does not put into words.
The two brothers work side by side to restore the vineyard to its former productivity.
The neighbors' predictions of ruin have discouraged Anselm from tending the vines.
Frey's tender memories of the vineyard drive him to labor alongside his brother.

questions.passage: In her later novels, the writer Cordelia Vance often withholds a character's decisive emotion, presenting instead some small external act that the reader must interpret. A scholar seeking to illustrate this indirection might quote the moment when ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Vance's work most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “She did not say she was afraid; she only turned the lamp a little higher, though the room was already bright.”
“‘I have never been so frightened in all my life,’ she confessed, trembling as she spoke.”
“The narrator explains that years of hardship had taught her to master every outward sign of feeling.”
“He watched her go, and wondered whether she had ever loved him at all.”

questions.passage: The naturalist Hollis Beckett rarely asserts a conclusion outright; instead she poses a question, lets the evidence accumulate, and allows readers to feel they have reached the verdict themselves. A critic wishing to demonstrate this method might cite the passage in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Beckett's writing most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Why, then, do the tunneling species alone possess this thickened membrane? Consider first the burrow's stale air; consider next the animal's labored breathing; and consider, finally, what such a membrane would spare it.”
“It is beyond dispute that the thickened membrane evolved as an adaptation to the low-oxygen air of the burrow.”
“The thickened membrane, as every student of the group knows, is among the most closely studied structures in the literature.”
“I confess I find the question of the membrane's origin too vexed to permit any confident answer.”

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • A 2020 study measured the resting metabolic rate of two lizard species.
  • Species A is active during the day (diurnal); Species B is active at night (nocturnal).
  • At 30°C, Species A's resting metabolic rate was 0.42 mL O2 per gram per hour.
  • At 30°C, Species B's resting metabolic rate was 0.19 mL O2 per gram per hour.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference between the two species' resting metabolic rates. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A 2020 study measured the resting metabolic rates of two lizard species, one diurnal and one nocturnal.
At 30°C, the diurnal Species A had a resting metabolic rate more than twice that of the nocturnal Species B (0.42 versus 0.19 mL O2 per gram per hour).
Species A is active during the day, whereas Species B is active at night.
At 30°C, the nocturnal Species B had a resting metabolic rate of 0.19 mL O2 per gram per hour.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Antikythera mechanism (Greek, about 100 BCE) used bronze gears to model astronomical cycles.
  • The Su Song clock (Chinese, 1088 CE) used an escapement to drive an astronomical model.
  • Both devices were long thought to be unique inventions with no precedents.
  • Recent scholarship has identified earlier, simpler geared and escapement devices in each culture.
questions.question: The student wants to present a generalization about the two devices that is supported by the notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Antikythera mechanism used bronze gears, whereas the Su Song clock used an escapement.
Once regarded as isolated inventions, both the Antikythera mechanism and the Su Song clock now appear to have grown out of earlier traditions of similar devices.
The Su Song clock, built in 1088 CE, was used to model astronomical cycles.
Recent scholarship has transformed the way historians understand ancient technology.

Halley's Comet, which returns roughly every 76 years, was most recently visible in 1986.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Tardigrades are microscopic animals, often nicknamed “water bears.”
  • They can survive extreme cold, intense radiation, and even the vacuum of space.
  • They enter a dormant state called cryptobiosis, losing almost all of their body water.
  • In cryptobiosis, their metabolism slows to less than 0.01% of its normal rate.
  • Researchers study them to understand the limits of life.
questions.question: The student wants to introduce tardigrades to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In cryptobiosis, a tardigrade's metabolism slows to less than 0.01% of normal as it loses nearly all of its body water.
Researchers study tardigrades in order to understand the limits of life.
Tardigrades enter a dormant state that biologists call cryptobiosis.
Tardigrades are microscopic animals, nicknamed “water bears,” that can survive extremes—cold, radiation, even the vacuum of space—that would kill almost any other creature.

  • Language Q: about 250 million speakers; 1.8 meaningful parts per word.
  • Language R: about 40 million speakers; 3.0 meaningful parts per word.

Word structure was measured as the average number of morphemes per word in each language.

questions.passage: Critics once read the novel's abrupt ending as a failure of craft, evidence that its author had simply lost control of the material. More recent readings treat the same abruptness as deliberate—a formal enactment of the very rupture the story describes. What one generation heard as a flaw, another has learned to hear as design.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It restates the earlier critical view in order to defend it against newer readings.
It supplies biographical evidence about the author's intentions for the ending.
It introduces a reinterpretation that reverses an earlier judgment, a reinterpretation the final sentence then endorses.
It concedes that the novel's ending is, after all, a genuine failure of craft.

questions.passage: For a century, the standard account held that a certain ancient script had been deciphered by a lone amateur working from a single bilingual inscription. Newly published correspondence, however, shows that dozens of scholars had circulated partial readings for decades beforehand, and that the amateur drew heavily on their unacknowledged work. The decipherment, it now appears, was less a solitary triumph than the visible endpoint of a long collective effort.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a scholarly method, illustrates it with an example, and then evaluates the method's limitations.
It poses a question, surveys several competing answers, and then defends one of them.
It introduces a discovery, explains its significance, and then predicts its future applications.
It presents a widely held account, introduces evidence that undercuts it, and then offers a revised understanding.

questions.passage: This essay does not attempt to settle whether the disputed painting is authentic. Its aim is narrower and, I hope, more useful: to show that the criteria critics have used to argue the question—brushwork, pigment, provenance—each rest on assumptions that the case itself calls into doubt. Until those assumptions are examined, further argument about the attribution is premature.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To demonstrate, on the basis of brushwork and pigment, that the disputed painting is authentic.
To compare the relative reliability of brushwork, pigment, and provenance as tests of authenticity.
To argue that the debate over the painting's authenticity rests on criteria whose assumptions must be scrutinized before the debate can advance.
To trace the history of the controversy surrounding the painting's attribution.

questions.passage: A paleontologist argues that a set of parallel scratch marks on fossil bones were made by stone tools, and therefore that hominins butchered the animal. The marks' straight, evenly spaced form, she contends, could only have been produced by a deliberately wielded implement. If she is right, the bones push back the earliest evidence of tool use by half a million years.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the underlined claim?
options: Stone tools capable of leaving such marks have been recovered from sites of comparable age on other continents.
The fossil bones belong to a species that hominins of the period are otherwise known to have hunted.
Trampling by hoofed animals on gritty ground has been shown to produce straight, evenly spaced marks indistinguishable from those made by stone tools.
Marks left by stone tools tend to be straighter when the tool is wielded deliberately than when it slips by accident.

questions.passage: Economists distinguish between risk, where the odds of each outcome are known, and uncertainty, where they are not. A card game played with a standard deck involves risk; the launch of a genuinely novel product involves uncertainty. Blurring the two, some argue, leads firms to trust probabilistic models in exactly the situations those models are least equipped to handle.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers evidence that the distinction drawn in the preceding sentence is untenable.
It restates the final sentence's warning in more concrete terms.
It introduces a third category beyond the two defined in the preceding sentence.
It illustrates the distinction drawn in the preceding sentence with a contrasting pair of examples.

questions.passage: We are told to read only the best books, and the counsel is good; yet it is offered as though the best books were a fixed and public catalogue, the same for every reader. But a book that rouses one mind to its finest activity may leave another merely respectful and asleep. The best books, rightly understood, are not a list to be handed down but a discovery each reader must make, and remake, for himself.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Readers should confine their attention to the books that have long been regarded as classics.
Which books count as the best depends on the individual reader, so each person must determine them anew.
Most readers are poor judges of which books will benefit them the most.
The best books are simply those that command the most widespread and lasting respect.

questions.passage: A geneticist proposes that a particular gene variant spread through a human population not because it aided survival directly but because it happened to lie very close, on the chromosome, to a different variant that was strongly favored—so that the two were usually inherited together. On this hypothesis, the first variant's frequency rose only as a byproduct of selection on its neighbor.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the geneticist's hypothesis?
options: The first variant produces a protein whose function is essential to survival in cold climates.
In populations where recombination had separated the two variants, the first variant conferred no survival advantage and did not increase in frequency.
The favored neighboring variant arose more recently than the first variant did.
In a closely related species, the two variants are located on different chromosomes.

questions.passage:

  • Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated species independently evolve similar traits.

  • The resemblance arose because both lineages adapted to the same aquatic environment.
questions.question: The student wants to explain convergent evolution to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In convergent evolution, unrelated species independently develop similar traits under similar pressures—as when sharks (fish) and dolphins (mammals), whose common ancestor had neither, both evolved streamlined bodies and fins for fast swimming.
The most recent common ancestor of sharks and dolphins had neither a streamlined body nor fins.
Sharks are fish, whereas dolphins are mammals, and the two are only distantly related.
Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated species independently evolve similar traits.

In a 2022 experiment, participants were randomly assigned to read in silence, with instrumental music, or with lyrical music.

Background music can affect how well people comprehend what they read.
